content:
I find myself with the setup below where I know some result holds for a basis of an algebra/module and I want to extend it to the entire space. In particular, the action of the algebra is linear in both arguments over the base field and the function I am interested in is also (bi)linear by construction as something extended from the basis.

-- Given a field,
variable (R : Type) [Field R]
-- an algebra over that field,
variable (A : Type) [Semiring A] [Algebra R A]
-- and a module over that algebra,
variable (M : Type) [AddCommGroup M] [Module R M] [Module A M]
-- such that for some finite sets of indices,
variable (ιₐ ιₘ : Type) [Fintype ιₐ] [Fintype ιₘ]
-- we have bases of the algebra and the module indexed by those sets,
variable (bₐ : Module.Basis ιₐ R A) (bₘ : Module.Basis ιₘ R M)
-- suppose that we have an action of the basis elements of A on the basis elements of M
variable (act : ιₐ → ιₘ → ιₘ)
-- and that this action is the same as the action of the algebra on the module.
variable (h : ∀ (ia : ιₐ) (im : ιₘ), (bₐ ia) • (bₘ im) = bₘ (act ia im))

-- Further, suppose we have a function from pairs of module basis vectors to the field,
variable (f : ιₘ → ιₘ → R)
-- such that it is invariant under the action of the algebra in the following sense:
variable (inv : ∀ (ia : ιₐ) (ix iy : ιₘ), f (act ia ix) iy = f ix (act ia iy))

-- Then the bilinear extension of this function to the whole module is also invariant
-- under the action:
example : ∀ (a : A) (x y : M) ,
    (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) (a • x) y =
    (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) x (a • y) := by
      sorry

-- Even a simpler step on one of the arguments is quite tricky
example : ∀ (ia : ιₐ) (ix : ιₘ) (y : M) ,
  (bₘ.constr R (f (act ia ix) ·)) y = (bₘ.constr R (f ix ·)) ((bₐ ia) • y) := by
    intro ia ix y
    calc
      (bₘ.constr R (f (act ia ix) ·)) y
          = (bₘ.constr R (f (act ia ix) ·)) (∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • bₘ y') := by rw[Module.Basis.sum_repr]
      _ = ∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • (bₘ.constr R (f (act ia ix) ·)) (bₘ y') := by rw[map_sum]; simp
      _ = ∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • (f (act ia ix) y') := by simp only [Module.Basis.constr_basis]
      _ = ∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • (f ix (act ia y')) := by simp[inv]
      _ = ∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • (bₘ.constr R (f ix ·)) (bₘ (act ia y')) := by simp only [Module.Basis.constr_basis]
      _ = (bₘ.constr R (f ix ·)) (∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • bₘ (act ia y')) := by simp
      _ = (bₘ.constr R (f ix ·)) (∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • (bₐ ia) • (bₘ y')) := by simp only[h]
      _ = (bₘ.constr R (f ix ·)) ((bₐ ia) • ∑ y', (bₘ.repr y) y' • (bₘ y')) := by rw [Finset.smul_sum]; congr; funext x; sorry
      -- Oh no! I need to prove (bₘ.repr y) x • bₐ ia • bₘ x = bₐ ia • (bₘ.repr y) x • bₘ x which I believe comes from
      -- `IsScalarTower R A M` but I don't know where to find that.
      _ = (bₘ.constr R (f ix ·)) ((bₐ ia) • y) := by simp

I have two problems. The first seems conceptual. I've defined [Module R M] and [Module A M] to state that both MMM and AAA are RRR-modules. However, it is stronger than this. Whenever a human hears that they think that AAA and MMM are RRR-modules in a compatible manner. That is, the action rm=(r1A)mr m = (r 1_A) mrm=(r1A​)m.

Is this what IsScalarTower is trying to convey? Where do I get myself an instance of that which recognises the Algebra.algebraMap? If I just add a variable [IsScalarTower R A M] how does it know to use this action. I suppose I'm asking, how does it find the correct instances of [SMul R M] and [SMul A M]. What if I happened to have two actions of AAA on MMM so that there were two instances of [Module A M]?

The second is more how much of a chore this is. Is there some tactic that knows to try expanding things out in basis vectors and simplify the sums by pulling out the scalars and summation from within linear maps? In particular, if there is an expression that is linear on the left hand side and one that is linear on the right hand side in a variable of my choosing, can I get the equivalent statement just for the basis vector.

I think this is what docs#Module.Basis.ext is trying to do, but I have a lot of trouble converting an expression like (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) (a • x) y into a linear function of y. How should one go about that? My first thought was to only intro ia ix and then funext_iff.mp but that asks for equality of functions, not linear functions.

Robert Spencer said:

What if I happened to have two actions of AAA on MMM so that there were two instances of [Module A M]?

You step back and remove one of them :)

Lean type classes expect only one correct instance for each type class search.

IsScalarTower means that the (expected to be unique) scalar multiplications are compatible
Though the "oh no" comment suggests you may be looking for docs#SMulCommClass instead

You step back and remove one of them :)

So if I had two compatible actions (i.e. the same field tower action) on MMM through AAA, I should define two morally different types M1M_1M1​ and M2M_2M2​ and instantiate separate Module A M for them? Even if they are both, say ℂ, I should create a newtype for that?

you may be looking for docs#SMulCommClass instead

Indeed - replacing sorry with rw[SMulCommClass.smul_comm] finished the proof.

Its still a very long and arduous computation though

Robert Spencer said:

You step back and remove one of them :)

So if I had two compatible actions (i.e. the same field tower action) on MMM through AAA, I should define two morally different types M1M_1M1​ and M2M_2M2​ and instantiate separate Module A M for them? Even if they are both, say ℂ, I should create a newtype for that?

if they're compatible and they're both A acting on M then they're equal so I'm not sure what you're talking about, could you clarify?

Sorry compatible as in have the same action of the image of $R$ in $A$ on $M$, i.e. both are linear maps under the same realisation of $M$ as a $R$-module (though now I realise there "is only one" action of $R$ on $M$?). Not equal though. For example the trivial and sign representations of the symmetric group algebra.

so M is an R-module and you have two different actions of A on M that extend the action of R? In that case I don't think typeclass will be happy if you make both of those actions into Module A M instances at the same time
You're already going to have difficulties even writing your different actions, because they'd both be a • x

Right. That makes sense. I suppose its shorthand one might use in writing: instead of saying "consider a representation that is isomorphic as a vector space to the complex numbers and carries the action ..." to just say "consider the action on the complex numbers"

In that case I still have my question about how to write some expression like (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) (a • x) y as a linear function of, say, a, so that I may apply Basis.ext on it.

Ruben Van de Velde said:

Though the "oh no" comment suggests you may be looking for docs#SMulCommClass instead

I'd hope that would follow from IsScalarTower since A is an R-algebra so R acts centrally on A

Robert Spencer said:

In that case I still have my question about how to write some expression like (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) (a • x) y as a linear function of, say, a, so that I may apply Basis.ext on it.

should be something like (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))).flip y ∘ₗ (LinearMap.id.smulRight x)
I did get SMulCommClass from the IsScalarTower instance, I just had to explicitly rw[SMulCommClass.smul_comm] in the end: simp wouldn't pick it up for example.

I see. It was a couple of magic incantations that I needed to learn, such as flip, LinearMap.smulRight and DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply for the other argument (a bit sad it isn't called LinearMap.smulLeft), but after a lot of wrangling I managed this monstrosity

example : ∀ (a : A) (x y : M) ,
    (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) (a • x) y =
    (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) x (a • y) := by
      intro a x y
      -- Turn everything into a linear map of a
      conv_rhs => {
        rw [←LinearMap.id_apply (R:=R) a ]
        rw [←LinearMap.smulRight_apply (LinearMap.id (R:=R)) y]
      }
      conv_lhs => {
        rw [←LinearMap.flip_apply]
        rw [←LinearMap.id_apply (R:=R) a ]
        rw [←LinearMap.smulRight_apply (LinearMap.id (R:=R)) x]
      }
      repeat rw[←LinearMap.comp_apply]
      -- Now show we just need to show it on basis vectors
      apply LinearMap.ext_iff.mp
      apply bₐ.ext
      intro ia
      -- For pedagogy an my sanity, put everything back
      repeat rw[LinearMap.comp_apply]
      conv_lhs => {
        rw [LinearMap.smulRight_apply (LinearMap.id (R:=R)) x]
        rw [LinearMap.id_apply (R:=R)]
        rw [LinearMap.flip_apply]
      }
      conv_rhs => {
        rw [LinearMap.smulRight_apply (LinearMap.id (R:=R)) y]
        rw [LinearMap.id_apply (R:=R)  ]
      }
      -- Now repeat for y
      conv_lhs => {
        rw [←DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]
      }
      conv_rhs => {
        rw [←DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]
      }
      repeat rw [←LinearMap.comp_apply]
      apply LinearMap.ext_iff.mp
      apply bₘ.ext
      intro iy
      repeat rw [LinearMap.comp_apply]
      conv_lhs => {
        rw [DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]
      }
      conv_rhs => {
        rw [DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]
      }
      -- Now repeat for x
      conv_rhs => {
        rw [←LinearMap.flip_apply]
      }
      conv_lhs => {
        rw [←LinearMap.flip_apply]
        rw [←DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]
        rw [←LinearMap.comp_apply]
      }
      apply LinearMap.ext_iff.mp
      apply bₘ.ext
      intro ib
      repeat rw [LinearMap.comp_apply]
      rw [DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]
      repeat rw[LinearMap.flip_apply]
      -- Now we actually prove the theorem
      repeat rw[h]
      repeat rw [Module.Basis.constr_basis]
      apply inv

I suppose I think it would be neat if there was a tactic or something that would rw the smulRight_apply and toLinearMap_apply and then apply b.ext and then undo what it did - my proof is pretty mechanical once you know the spells, and it would be nice to be able to say "get me this expression as a linear function applied to y" or some other variable I specify. I'm guessing such a thing doesn't exist.
Rather than finding the lemmas to rewrite into a point-free expression, you'd probably do better to just use a suffices to write it out explicitly

Aha. Even better. Something like

example : ∀ (a : A) (x y : M) ,
    (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) (a • x) y =
    (bₘ.constr R (fun i => bₘ.constr R (f i ·))) x (a • y) := by
      intro a x y
      convert_to
        (((bₘ.constr R) fun i ↦ (bₘ.constr R) fun x ↦ f i x).flip y ∘ₗ LinearMap.id.smulRight x) a =
        (((bₘ.constr R) fun i ↦ (bₘ.constr R) fun x ↦ f i x) x ∘ₗ LinearMap.id.smulRight y) a
      apply LinearMap.ext_iff.mp
      apply bₐ.ext
      intro ia
      convert_to
        ((((bₘ.constr R) fun i ↦ (bₘ.constr R) fun x ↦ f i x) ∘ₗ DistribSMul.toLinearMap R M (bₐ ia)) x) y =
        (((bₘ.constr R) fun i ↦ (bₘ.constr R) fun x ↦ f i x) x ∘ₗ DistribSMul.toLinearMap R M (bₐ ia)) y
      apply LinearMap.ext_iff.mp
      apply bₘ.ext
      intro iy
      convert_to
        (((bₘ.constr R) fun i ↦ (bₘ.constr R) fun x ↦ f i x).flip (bₘ iy) ∘ₗ DistribSMul.toLinearMap R M (bₐ ia)) x =
        (((bₘ.constr R) fun i ↦ (bₘ.constr R) fun x ↦ f i x).flip (bₐ ia • bₘ iy)) x
      apply LinearMap.ext_iff.mp
      apply bₘ.ext
      intro ib
      simp only [LinearMap.flip_apply, h, Module.Basis.constr_basis, inv, LinearMap.comp_apply,
                 DistribSMul.toLinearMap_apply R M (s:= bₐ ia)]

then works.

Thanks!
